content.rendered:
Home/Privacy Policy

Privacy Policy

Last updated: January 2026

★★★★★ 5.0 Google reviews Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider Same working day response London & Hertfordshire

This Privacy Policy explains how Whizz Solutions Ltd (“WhizzIT”, “we”, “us”) collects, uses and protects the personal information you provide when you use our website or engage our managed IT services. We are committed to protecting your privacy and handling your data in an open and transparent manner, in line with UK data protection law including the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018.

Who we are

Whizz Solutions Ltd is a managed IT services provider based in London and Hertfordshire. For any privacy-related questions you can contact us at info@whizzit.co.uk or by post at 124 City Rd, London, EC1V 2NX.

Information we collect

  • Contact details you provide via our forms, such as your name, email address, phone number and company name.
  • Enquiry details, the content of any message you send us.
  • Technical data, such as IP address, browser type and usage data collected through cookies and analytics (see our Cookie Policy).

How we use your information

  • To respond to your enquiries and provide the services you request.
  • To manage and deliver our managed IT services to clients.
  • To improve our website and understand how visitors use it.
  • To send relevant service updates where you have agreed to receive them.

Lawful basis

We process your personal data on the basis of your consent, the performance of a contract, and our legitimate interests in operating and promoting our business. You may withdraw consent at any time by contacting us.

Sharing your information

We do not sell your personal data. We may share it with trusted service providers who help us operate our business (for example email, hosting and analytics providers), all of whom are required to keep it secure and use it only for the purposes we specify.

Data retention

We keep personal data only for as long as necessary to fulfil the purposes for which it was collected, including to satisfy any legal, accounting or reporting requirements.

Your rights

Under UK data protection law you have the right to access, correct, erase, restrict or object to the processing of your personal data, and the right to data portability. To exercise any of these rights, contact us at info@whizzit.co.uk. You also have the right to lodge a complaint with the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) at ico.org.uk.

Security

We take appropriate technical and organisational measures to safeguard your personal data against unauthorised access, loss or misuse.

Changes to this policy

We may update this Privacy Policy from time to time. Any changes will be posted on this page with an updated revision date.

This policy is provided as a starting template and should be reviewed by a qualified professional before publication to ensure it reflects your specific data-processing practices.

Ready when you are
Questions about your data?

If you want to know what we hold, why we hold it, or you would like it removed, just ask.

Overview

Get the foundations right

Everything on your network depends on the cabling underneath it. Poor or improvised cabling causes intermittent faults that are painful to diagnose and expensive to live with.

WhizzIT designs and installs structured cabling done properly, the right cable for the job, neat comms rooms, clear labelling and full testing and certification, so your network has a foundation you can rely on and easily extend.

Cabling is planned, installed and certified to standard, with the documentation handed over so future work does not start with guesswork. Everything runs through the same UK service desk that handles your day-to-day tickets, so there is no separate team to chase. Across 2025 our average first response time was 9 minutes and our average resolution time was 6 hours, measured across every ticket we handled. We are a team of five engineers supporting more than 30 UK businesses, from two-user teams to organisations of 150+ users.

Back to Network Management

What’s included

  • Cabling design and site survey
  • Cat6, Cat6a and fibre optic cabling
  • Patch panels and comms cabinets
  • Neat cable management and labelling
  • Testing and certification
  • Office moves, fit-outs and expansions
Why cabling causes strange faults

Intermittent problems usually start underneath

Cabling faults rarely announce themselves. They surface as a call that drops once a day, a machine that negotiates at a tenth of its speed, or a camera that goes offline when the heating runs. Because the symptoms look like software, teams often spend weeks in the wrong place before anyone tests the cable.

A tester that lights up green confirms continuity. Certification measures the things that actually degrade performance: crosstalk, return loss, attenuation and length, against the standard for the category installed. It is also the only evidence that the installation met specification on the day, which matters when a fault appears two years later and nobody can agree what was installed.

Cabling outlives several generations of the equipment plugged into it, so the sensible question is not what today’s switches need but what the building will need before it is next refitted. The cost difference between categories is small next to the cost of pulling cable through an occupied building a second time.

Heat, dust and improvisation account for a large share of hardware failures. A rack in a cupboard with no ventilation will shorten the life of everything in it, and a rack with no patching discipline turns a five-minute change into an afternoon. Ventilation, power, containment and labelling are not tidiness for its own sake; they decide how long a fault takes to find.

An unlabelled patch field means every future change begins with tracing. A documented schedule mapping outlet to patch panel to switch port turns that into a two-minute job. It is the cheapest thing to do during installation and the most expensive to reconstruct afterwards.

Planning an installation

The disruptive part is access, not the cable

Most of the work in an occupied building is about getting to places: ceilings, risers, and rooms that can only be entered outside business hours. Agreeing routes, containment and access windows before starting is what keeps an installation from becoming a series of interruptions, and it is the part most often underestimated when a date is promised.

New sites and fit-outs are considerably cheaper to cable before fit-out finishes than after, so this is worth raising early in any move. Cabling underpins everything else on the network, particularly business Wi-Fi, where access point positions dictate where outlets must land.

Overview

Connectivity you can count on

When your internet drops, so does your business, cloud apps, email, phones and card payments all rely on it. A single connection with no backup is a single point of failure.

WhizzIT sources and manages the right connectivity for each site, adds automatic failover, and uses SD-WAN to intelligently route traffic across links, so you get resilient, prioritised, always-on connectivity you don’t have to think about.

Connectivity is designed around how your sites actually communicate, then managed as one service rather than several separate supplier relationships. It is priced per user at a fixed monthly cost rather than bundled into rigid packages, so it scales with your team. Everything runs through the same UK service desk that handles your day-to-day tickets, so there is no separate team to chase. Back to Network Management

What’s included

  • Leased lines and business broadband

  • SD-WAN for intelligent, resilient routing
  • Multi-site and branch connectivity
  • Traffic prioritisation (QoS) for voice and cloud
  • Monitoring and managed support
How resilience actually works

Two lines are not resilience if they share a duct

Buying a second connection feels like buying resilience, and often is not. If both circuits run from the same exchange, along the same route, or terminate on the same piece of your equipment, one contractor with a digger takes out both. Diversity has to be designed rather than assumed.

Genuine resilience means the two services do not share a failure point: different providers where possible, physically different routes into the building, and separate terminating equipment. Where a truly diverse fixed route is not available at a site, 4G or 5G backup gives you a path that fails independently by definition, because it does not use the ground at all.

The value is in how fast and how quietly the switch happens. A failover that drops every call and every session is better than an outage, but only just. SD-WAN monitors the health of each path continuously and moves traffic when a link degrades, not only when it dies completely, which matters because slow and lossy is more common than fully down.

A voice call is ruined by 100ms of jitter that a file upload would never notice. Policy-based routing lets you put real-time traffic on the most stable path and bulk transfers on the cheaper one, and change that automatically when conditions shift. This is the part that a straight second line cannot do at all.

Most sites that feel slow are not short of bandwidth. They are suffering from contention at peak times, a saturated upload path, or one backup job running in business hours. Measuring before upgrading usually costs less than upgrading, and sometimes shows the circuit was never the constraint.

Contracts and practicalities

Lead times decide project dates more often than budgets

New fixed circuits are quoted in weeks and occasionally months, particularly where a new fibre build or a wayleave from a landlord is involved. Anyone planning a move, a fit-out or a new site should start connectivity first and everything else around it, because it is the one element that cannot be compressed by working harder.

We source and manage the circuits rather than leaving you to hold the carrier relationship, so a fault is our call to make and chase. Connectivity sits alongside managed firewall at the network edge, and the monitoring that proves a link is degrading is covered by network monitoring.

Overview

Catch problems before your team does

Most network outages give warning signs long before they bring things to a halt, if someone is watching. Without monitoring, the first you hear of a problem is when work stops.

WhizzIT provides continuous, proactive monitoring and management of your network infrastructure, with alerting, performance analytics and the hands-on management to act on what we see.

Monitoring runs continuously across your network hardware and connectivity, and alerts land in the same helpdesk queue our engineers already work to. WhizzIT is Cyber Essentials certified and a Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider, so our security fundamentals are independently assessed rather than simply claimed. It is priced per user at a fixed monthly cost rather than bundled into rigid packages, so it scales with your team. What’s included

  • 24/7 monitoring of switches, routers and firewalls
  • Connectivity and uptime monitoring
  • Proactive alerting and issue resolution
  • Performance and bandwidth analytics
  • Capacity planning and recommendations
  • Regular reporting and reviews
What monitoring is for

An alert nobody acts on is just a log entry

Monitoring tools are easy to buy and easy to ignore. The difference between a dashboard and a service is whether an alert reaches a person who is expected to do something about it, within a time you have agreed. Everything else is decoration.

Out of the box, most monitoring alerts on values that mean nothing in your environment, and the team learns within a fortnight to dismiss them. Once that habit forms, the genuine alert is dismissed too. Tuning thresholds to what is normal for each device, and deliberately alerting on less, is what keeps the alerts worth reading.

Hardware rarely fails without warning. Rising interface errors on a switch port, a firewall session table filling steadily, a failing power supply in a resilient pair, disk latency creeping up, an access point rebooting nightly: each of these is visible days ahead if something is watching. That window is the entire argument for monitoring.

When someone asks whether the connection needs upgrading or whether the switch stack will cope with thirty more staff, the honest answer requires months of trend data. Monitoring that only shows the present moment can describe a problem but cannot support a purchase decision, which is where most of the budget conversations actually happen.

Monitoring depends on an accurate inventory, and inventories drift. Devices get added during a project and never recorded, or replaced without the record being updated. Reconciling what is discovered on the network against what is documented is unglamorous and routinely finds equipment nobody had accounted for.

Monitoring versus management

Watching and fixing are different commitments

Plenty of arrangements notify you and stop there, which leaves the work exactly where it was. We act on what the monitoring shows: applying firmware updates in agreed windows, replacing hardware showing early failure, chasing the carrier when a circuit degrades, and reporting on what changed rather than only on what broke.

Monitoring the network is one layer. Security monitoring of endpoints and identity is a different discipline and is covered by managed detection and response, while the edge devices being watched here are configured and maintained under managed firewall.

Overview

A firewall that’s actually managed

A firewall is only as good as its configuration and upkeep. Left unmanaged, rules drift, firmware falls behind and gaps quietly open, exactly what attackers look for.

WhizzIT takes ownership of your next-generation firewall end to end: correct configuration, active threat prevention, timely updates and continuous monitoring, so your perimeter stays strong without adding to your team’s workload.

Firewalls are configured, monitored and kept patched as an ongoing service, with rule changes handled by us rather than left to accumulate untracked. We are a team of five engineers supporting more than 30 UK businesses, from two-user teams to organisations of 150+ users. WhizzIT is Cyber Essentials certified and a Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider, so our security fundamentals are independently assessed rather than simply claimed. It is priced per user at a fixed monthly cost rather than bundled into rigid packages, so it scales with your team.

Back to Network Management

What’s included

  • Next-generation firewall supply, setup and configuration
  • Security rule and policy management
  • Intrusion prevention and threat filtering
  • Secure site-to-site and remote-access VPN
  • Firmware patching and updates
  • 24/7 monitoring, alerting and reporting
The problem

Having a firewall is not the same as being protected

Almost every business we assess already owns a capable firewall. The box is rarely the issue. What it is running, and who last looked at it, usually is.

Firewall vulnerabilities get published, and because these devices sit on the public internet they are scanned and exploited quickly, sometimes within days of an advisory. An unpatched firewall is not a neutral risk, it is an internet-facing door with a known key. Yet firmware updates get deferred because nobody wants to reboot the internet during working hours, and then the deferral becomes permanent.

Somebody opened a port temporarily for a supplier in 2021 and it is still open. An any to any rule went in to get a project finished and never came out. Nobody can say which rules are still needed because there is no record of why they were added, so nobody dares remove any of them.

The intrusion prevention, web filtering and threat intelligence that make a next-generation firewall worth buying are licensed separately. When those lapse the device carries on passing traffic quite happily with its best features switched off, and nothing tells you.

What we take ownership of

  • Firmware patching on a managed schedule
  • Rule review with a documented reason for each
  • Intrusion prevention and web filtering kept licensed
  • Site to site and remote access VPN
  • Logging retained so incidents can be investigated
  • Monitoring and alerting on device health
Capability

What next-generation actually means

The phrase is on every vendor’s datasheet. These are the parts that earn it.

Application awareness

Older firewalls made decisions on ports. Modern traffic mostly rides over 443, so port rules tell you almost nothing. Application control identifies what is really passing through, which is how you allow a service you sanction while blocking one you do not, even though both look identical from the outside.

Intrusion prevention

Inspects traffic for known exploit patterns and blocks them in transit. It is one of the licensed features that quietly stops working when a subscription lapses, which is why we track renewals as part of the service rather than leaving it to a diary entry.

Encrypted traffic inspection

Most threats now arrive over encrypted connections, so a firewall that cannot look inside them is guessing. It is worth being straight about the trade-offs: inspection costs throughput, needs certificates deploying properly, and some traffic such as banking should be excluded deliberately. Done carelessly it breaks applications, which is why it is configured deliberately rather than switched on wholesale.

Remote access

VPN, or something better than VPN

Traditional VPN does one thing: it puts a remote device on your network. That was fine when the alternative was nothing, and it is now the part of the setup attackers most want to reach, because one stolen laptop or one reused password buys them the whole internal network to explore.

The direction of travel is access to specific applications rather than access to the network. A user is authenticated, their device is checked, and they are connected to the one system they need and nothing else. If that account is later compromised, the damage is bounded by design instead of by luck. Not every business needs to move immediately, but if your VPN currently drops everyone onto a flat internal network, that is worth revisiting.

Multi-factor authentication on VPN access without exception, accounts removed the day someone leaves rather than the following quarter, and internal segmentation so a compromised machine cannot reach your servers and your backups just because it is inside the building. We are a Fortinet partner and will recommend the right model for your size and connectivity rather than the box with the best margin.

Wireless that just works, everywhere

Patchy Wi-Fi, dead spots and a network everyone shares with guests are more than an annoyance, they cost time and create security risk.

WhizzIT designs wireless around your actual building and how you work: a proper site survey, business-grade access points, separate secure networks for staff and guests, and seamless roaming so devices stay connected as people move around.

Wireless is designed from a site survey of your actual building rather than a floor plan, then monitored once it is live so degradation is spotted before people complain. Why coverage maps mislead

Full signal bars and unusable Wi-Fi are compatible

A device showing four bars is reporting how loudly it can hear the access point, not whether it can hold a usable conversation with it. Most complaints about bad Wi-Fi come from environments with plenty of signal and too much interference, too many clients per radio, or access points shouting over each other.

Plasterboard is nearly transparent to Wi-Fi; concrete, foil-backed insulation, plant rooms, lift shafts and metal racking are not. Older buildings with thick walls and modern buildings with foil-lined insulation both cause problems, for opposite reasons. This is why a survey in the actual building beats a plan drawn from a floor plan.

Adding units to fix a dead spot frequently degrades the whole floor, because neighbouring access points on overlapping channels interfere with each other. Correct channel planning and turning power down rather than up is usually what fixes a struggling network. Density needs designing, not increasing.

A single shared network means a guest laptop sits alongside your file server and your card terminal. Separate networks for staff, guests and equipment such as printers, cameras and building systems keeps a compromised or simply infected visitor device away from everything that matters, and lets you apply different rules to each.

A pre-shared key known to every current and former member of staff cannot be revoked for one person, so in practice it never changes. Per-user authentication removes that problem entirely and means access ends when employment does, which is also the answer to the question an auditor will eventually ask.

Manufacturing and engineering

Two networks, one business: the office and the shop floor

Manufacturers run two quite different technology estates. The office side looks like any other business. The production side runs machine controllers, PLCs and inspection equipment, often on operating systems that cannot be patched and were never designed to be on a network at all.

A press brake or CNC controller running an unsupported Windows version usually cannot be updated without invalidating the machine’s support agreement. The workable answer is to isolate it: a separate network segment, tightly controlled routes in and out, and monitoring on the boundary rather than on the machine.

In an office, a slow morning is an irritation. On a line, stoppage has a number attached and it is usually already calculated. That changes the priority conversation: resilience spending on the things that halt production is far easier to justify than a general upgrade.

Steel racking, machinery and vehicle movement break wireless coverage in ways an office survey never predicts. Scanners, tablets and terminals need a network designed for the building as it actually is, which means surveying the space rather than assuming it.

What makes IT different in a law firm

A practice runs on confidentiality, an audit trail and files that have to survive for decades. That combination puts different demands on IT than almost any other professional service, and it is where most generic support arrangements fall short.

Interception of completion emails and last-minute changes of bank details is one of the most common frauds aimed at law firms, and it arrives through the mailbox rather than the firewall. The controls that matter are email authentication, impersonation protection, tight rules on who can change payment information, and training that teaches fee earners to verify by phone against a known number.

Wills, deeds and matter files often have to be produced long after the matter closed and long after the software that created them was retired. That is an archiving question rather than a backup question: readable formats, documented restore paths, and storage you can still search in fifteen years.

Time recording, matter files and the client account all live in the practice management system, so its availability effectively sets the firm’s working hours. Brokers, MGAs and insurers

The resilience you sell is the resilience you are judged on

Insurance businesses hold an unusual concentration of sensitive personal data and, in health and protection lines, special-category data too. They also occupy an awkward position: a broker whose systems are down is unavailable at exactly the moment a client needs to notify a claim.

Workload arrives in bursts around renewal dates and after weather events, and capacity has to be there on the day rather than on average. Monitoring that only reports monthly uptime will miss the hour that actually mattered.

Quoting, binding and claims handling all run through a mix of broker software and insurer extranets, each with its own authentication and browser quirks. Keeping that estate stable, patched and accessible is most of the practical support work in this sector.

Where medical or health information is held, the standard for who can see what stops being a matter of tidiness and becomes a matter of lawful basis. Role-based access, logging and reviewed permissions are the mechanics that make that defensible.

MGAs and brokers operating under delegated authority hold data the insurer remains accountable for, which means the insurer’s own assurance requirements land on your infrastructure. Expect questions about encryption, retention periods, sub-processors and breach notification timelines, and expect them in a questionnaire rather than a conversation. Having those answers documented in advance turns a two-week scramble into an afternoon.

Regulated financial services

Operational resilience is a regulatory expectation, not an IT preference

Financial services firms are held to a standard of resilience that most businesses are not. Since March 2022 FCA-regulated firms have been expected to identify their important business services, set impact tolerances for disruption and be able to show they can stay within them. That obligation reaches directly into IT.

The FCA expects firms to oversee outsourced arrangements rather than delegate the risk with the work. In practice that means your provider should be able to answer questions about access control, change management, incident response and where data physically sits, in writing and without a scramble. We keep that documentation current because it is asked for, not because it is a nice extra.

Communications retention, journalling and immutable copies are requirements before they are features, and they change how mailboxes, archives and backups should be configured. Getting this right at design time is far cheaper than reconstructing history later.

An impact tolerance you have never tested is an assumption. We would rather rehearse a restore against a defined recovery time and find the gaps in a planned exercise than discover them during an incident.

Regulators have grown wary of firms depending on a single provider for everything, and the same logic applies to the platforms underneath. Knowing which single points of failure exist between your desk and your client’s money, and having a documented answer for each, is a more useful exercise than adding another tool. We would rather map that honestly and tell you where the exposure sits than pretend a monitoring dashboard removes it.

Overview

Azure infrastructure, managed for you

Microsoft Azure gives you scalable, pay-as-you-go infrastructure, but it needs designing, securing and managing to deliver value without runaway cost.

WhizzIT designs, migrates and manages your Azure environment end to end, keeping it secure, optimised and aligned to what your business actually needs.

Azure environments are designed, deployed and then managed on an ongoing basis, including cost review, because unmanaged cloud spend climbs quietly. Everything runs through the same UK service desk that handles your day-to-day tickets, so there is no separate team to chase. Across 2025 our average first response time was 9 minutes and our average resolution time was 6 hours, measured across every ticket we handled. We are a team of five engineers supporting more than 30 UK businesses, from two-user teams to organisations of 150+ users. WhizzIT is Cyber Essentials certified and a Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider, so our security fundamentals are independently assessed rather than simply claimed.

Back to Managed Cloud Services

  • Azure architecture and deployment

Cost control

Why Azure bills surprise people

Azure is pay as you go, which sounds reassuring until the first bill arrives that nobody can explain. It is almost never one big mistake. It is a dozen small ones nobody owned.

Virtual machines get sized generously during a project and never revisited, so you pay for headroom you have never touched. Test environments spin up on a Tuesday and run all weekend because switching them off was somebody’s job in principle.

Disks and public IP addresses outlive the machines they belonged to and keep billing quietly on their own. Nothing is tagged, so when the bill goes up nobody can say which project or department caused it.

Running everything at pay as you go rates when the workload is clearly permanent is the most common overspend we find. Reservations and savings plans exist precisely for predictable workloads, and applying them properly is often the single biggest reduction available without changing a thing technically.

None of this needs heroics. It needs somebody looking every month, which is what management means in practice rather than in a brochure.

Where the money usually leaks

  • Virtual machines sized for a worst case that never arrives
  • Dev and test environments running outside working hours
  • Orphaned disks, snapshots and public IP addresses
  • Pay as you go rates on permanently running workloads
  • No tagging, so no accountability for spend
  • Data egress nobody budgeted for
What we run

The five things we actually do in Azure

This is the work we get asked for, so it is the work the page is about.

Migration

Moving servers and workloads off ageing on-premise hardware. Some things lift and shift unchanged, others are better re-platformed on the way across, and a few are genuinely better left where they are. We will tell you which is which rather than moving everything because it is billable.

Management and cost

Monitoring, patching, backups verified, capacity reviewed and spend examined every month. Right-sizing, reservations and switching off what nobody is using. This is the part that decides whether Azure saves you money or quietly costs more than the servers did.

Security

Identity first, because in Azure identity is the perimeter. Conditional access, multi-factor authentication, privileged access controlled rather than permanent, network segmentation, and alerting that reaches a human. We are Cyber Essentials Certified and apply the same standards here.

Backup and recovery

Backups configured, retained to a period you have actually chosen, held so ransomware cannot reach them, and tested by restoring rather than by looking at a green tick. Recovery objectives agreed per workload up front.

Virtual desktops

Azure Virtual Desktop where it genuinely fits, which is more often than people expect and less often than the marketing suggests. See below for the honest version.

Ongoing advice

As a Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider your licensing, support and escalation come direct from us rather than through a reseller chain, so when something needs Microsoft it goes to Microsoft.

Azure Virtual Desktop

Virtual desktops, honestly

Azure Virtual Desktop earns its place in specific situations, and it is worth being clear about which. It is excellent when you need people working on company systems from equipment you do not control, so contractors, offshore teams, personal machines and anyone using their own laptop. It keeps the data in Azure rather than on the endpoint, which is a genuine security win. It suits a legacy application that refuses to behave on modern desktops. It is also the fastest way to onboard twenty people at once without waiting on hardware.

It is excellent when you need people working on company systems from equipment you do not control, so contractors, offshore teams, personal machines and anyone using their own laptop. It keeps the data in Azure rather than on the endpoint. It also suits a legacy application that refuses to behave on modern desktops, and it is the fastest way to onboard twenty people without waiting on hardware.

It is not automatically cheaper than buying laptops. Session hosts are virtual machines and they bill while they run, so the cost case depends entirely on sizing them properly and letting autoscale shut capacity down outside working hours. Get that wrong and you have bought an expensive way to run Windows. Profiles matter too, because user data has to live somewhere sensible or logins slow to a crawl, which is what FSLogix profile containers are for.

If you already have Microsoft 365 Business Premium or a Windows E3 or E5 plan, the desktop entitlement is typically already included, so you are paying Azure for the compute and storage rather than buying a whole new product. We will work out whether the numbers land in your favour before recommending it, and say so if they do not.

Overview

Google doesn’t back up your data the way you think

Google Workspace keeps your data available, but it isn’t a backup. Accidental deletion, malicious action or a compromised account can lose data for good.

WhizzIT adds independent, automated backup for Gmail, Drive, Shared Drives, Contacts and Calendar, with fast, granular recovery when you need it.

Backup covers Gmail, Drive, Shared Drives and Calendar independently of Google’s own retention, so a deletion that falls outside those windows is still recoverable. We are a team of five engineers supporting more than 30 UK businesses, from two-user teams to organisations of 150+ users. WhizzIT is Cyber Essentials certified and a Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider, so our security fundamentals are independently assessed rather than simply claimed. Back to Managed Cloud Services

What’s included

  • Automated daily backup of Google Workspace
  • Gmail, Drive and Shared Drive protection
  • Contacts and Calendar backup
  • Granular, point-in-time recovery
  • Protection against accidental and malicious deletion
  • Retention aligned to your needs
Where the gap actually is

The bin empties, and that is by design

Google Workspace is genuinely resilient. Your data is replicated, the service stays up, and hardware failure is not something you need to think about. That is availability, and Google is clear that it is what they are responsible for. Retention is a different question, and the answer is a countdown rather than an archive.

Items removed from Gmail or Drive sit in trash for a limited period and are then purged. An administrator has a further short window to recover some of it, and after that the copy is gone rather than archived somewhere deeper. Most data loss we are called about is not dramatic: someone tidied a shared folder in good faith, and the discovery came weeks later when a colleague went looking for a file.

Files in a personal My Drive belong to that account. Suspend or delete the account without transferring ownership first and the files go with it, including anything they had shared with the team, which stops resolving for everyone else. Shared Drives avoid this because the team owns the content rather than an individual, but almost every business has years of work sitting in personal Drives regardless.

Accidental deletion is recoverable within the window. Deliberate deletion by someone who has taken over an account is designed to defeat exactly that, and emptying the trash is part of it. This is the case that separates a backup from a retention policy: an independent copy sits outside the account, so nothing done inside it can reach the copy.

Drive for desktop keeps local and cloud copies in step, which is the point of it. If files are encrypted on the laptop, the sync does its job and carries the damage upward. Point-in-time restore is what gets you back to the state before the change, rather than trying to unpick which version of which file is intact.

What good looks like

The test is the restore, not the backup

Backups fail quietly. They run, they report success, and the problem only shows up on the day someone needs a file back. That is why the measure worth caring about is whether a restore has actually been performed recently, not whether the job is green.

What we look for is granular recovery, so a single message or one folder can come back without restoring an entire account; coverage across Gmail, Drive, Shared Drives, Contacts and Calendar rather than mail alone; a retention period long enough that a deletion noticed months later is still recoverable; and a copy held independently of the Workspace tenant, so a compromise of the tenant cannot reach it.

Two practical questions are worth asking of any arrangement, including ours: how far back can you go, and how long would a realistic recovery take. If nobody can answer both, the position is not yet a backup. If you also run Microsoft, the same reasoning applies there and is covered by Microsoft 365 backup, with the broader plan in business continuity and disaster recovery.

Overview

Move to the cloud without the headaches

Migrations go wrong when they’re rushed or under-planned, lost data, downtime and frustrated staff. Done right, they’re barely noticeable.

As a Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider, WhizzIT plans and delivers migrations to Microsoft 365, Azure and Google Workspace carefully, with data integrity and continuity built in.

Migrations are planned around your working week and run in stages, so mailboxes, files and identities move without a weekend of downtime. Across 2025 our average first response time was 9 minutes and our average resolution time was 6 hours, measured across every ticket we handled. We are a team of five engineers supporting more than 30 UK businesses, from two-user teams to organisations of 150+ users. WhizzIT is Cyber Essentials certified and a Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider, so our security fundamentals are independently assessed rather than simply claimed.

Back to Managed Cloud Services

What’s included

  • Migration planning and readiness assessment
  • Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace migrations
  • Email, files and identity migration
  • Google-to-Microsoft 365 moves
  • Data integrity checks and validation
  • User communication and support
Timescales

How long a migration really takes

For around 50 users, budget roughly seven days of actual configuration work from us. Here is where that time goes.

01

Discovery and readiness

Before anything moves we find out what actually exists. How much mail and how many files, who owns the shared mailboxes nobody admits to using, which applications sign in with the old system, what state the devices are in. This is also where most nasty surprises get caught, while they are still cheap.

02

Build and pilot

We set up the new tenant properly, with security baselines, multi-factor authentication and licensing sorted from the start rather than retrofitted later. Then a small pilot group moves first. It is far better to find the awkward bits with four willing people than with all fifty at once.

03

Bulk move and cutover

Mail and files copy across in the background over several days while everyone carries on working in the old system. The switch itself is the short part, scheduled deliberately for a quiet window, followed by a few days of us being close by while people find the things only real use uncovers.

Seven days is the configuration effort, not the calendar. A 50 user move typically spans two to three weeks end to end, because the bulk copy runs in the background and the pilot needs a few days of real use before the rest follow.

Experience

Where migrations go wrong

Moving mailboxes is the easy bit. Almost every migration that goes badly goes badly for the same handful of reasons, and none of them are the mail.

Shared mailboxes, distribution lists and meeting rooms get forgotten because no single person owns them, then reappear the morning after cutover when nobody can book anything.

Permissions on shared folders are assumed to carry over neatly and rarely do, so somebody either loses access to a folder they need or quietly gains access to one they should not have. Third party applications that authenticate against the old system stop working until each one is reconnected, and the list of them is always longer than anyone expects.

Everyone remembers the laptops. Half the workforce has mail on a phone that nobody has recorded anywhere, and if that is not handled they spend cutover morning locked out and irritated. Old licences are the last one, still quietly billing months later because nobody cancelled them.

It just has to be written down beforehand and worked through, which is precisely what the discovery stage is for.

Caught during discovery

  • Shared mailboxes, distribution lists and meeting rooms
  • Folder permissions and who really needs what

A tenant does not stay tidy on its own

Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace are set up once, usually carefully, and then reality happens. People join and leave, someone shares a folder to get a job done on a Friday, a trial licence quietly becomes a renewal, an app gets granted access and is never looked at again. None of it is negligence. It is what a live system does when no one has been given the job of tending it.

Offboarding usually gets the obvious part right, which is disabling the sign-in. What tends to survive is everything attached to that person: files owned by their account, a shared mailbox they still have rights to, an app password issued years ago, a personal device still enrolled. The tidy version archives the mailbox, transfers ownership of their files to a named colleague, revokes tokens and sessions rather than only the password, and then releases the licence. Done in that order, nothing is lost and nothing is left open.

The common pattern is paying for more seats than people, while some of the people you do have sit on a licence tier above what their role needs, and a handful sit below what they actually use. Reviewing assignment against real usage two or three times a year usually pays for the review several times over. Anyone-with-the-link sharing is genuinely useful and genuinely hard to retire, because the link keeps working long after the project ends and nobody remembers creating it. Expiry dates on external shares, a periodic report of what is shared outside the business, and a default that favours named access over open links keep this manageable without making collaboration painful.

Someone signs in to a tool with their work account and grants it permission to read mail or files. That consent persists whether or not the tool is still in use, and it is not visible unless somebody looks. WhizzIT designs, implements and, crucially, tests your backup and disaster recovery, so you can recover fast with confidence. Untested backups are one of the most common gaps we find.

The two numbers

Two numbers decide everything

Before any of the technology matters, two questions need answering, and they are business questions rather than IT ones.

How much work can you afford to lose? That is your recovery point objective. If backups run nightly, your RPO is up to 24 hours, which means a failure at four in the afternoon costs you the whole day. For a finance team mid month that might be genuinely serious. For other work it is an annoyance. Only you can say which.

How long can you be down? That is your recovery time objective. Restoring a large fileserver from cloud storage is not quick, and if the honest answer is two days while the business needs four hours, no amount of backup software fixes that. The design has to change instead, usually towards replication or standby systems for the handful of things that genuinely cannot wait.

Get those two numbers agreed and everything else follows from them. Skip them and you end up with backups that technically exist and a recovery that takes a week, which is the situation most businesses are quietly in.

What we agree with you

  • Recovery point objective, per system
  • Recovery time objective, per system
  • What is genuinely critical and what can wait
  • Who does what during an incident
  • How often recovery is tested
  • Where the documentation lives when systems are down
Ransomware

Your backup is a target, not a safety net

Ransomware crews worked out years ago that encrypting live data is only half a job. If the victim can restore, they do not pay. So the backups get attacked first, and the tools people rely on most are the ones sitting on the same network with the same administrator credentials.

At least one copy has to be somewhere the attacker cannot touch. Immutable storage that cannot be altered or deleted for a set period, separate credentials that are not the ones your domain admin uses daily, and multi-factor authentication on the backup console itself. The old three copies, two media, one offsite rule still holds up, with the modern addition that one copy should be genuinely unchangeable.

Attackers commonly sit inside a network for weeks before triggering anything. If your retention is short, your clean restore point may already have been deleted by the time you need it. Retention is a security decision, not just a storage cost.

How ransomware targets backups
The gap almost everyone has

Microsoft 365 is not backing up your data

This one catches out well-run businesses regularly. Microsoft keeps your service running and protects its own infrastructure. It does not keep a point-in-time copy of your data for you to roll back to, and its own shared responsibility model says so plainly.

Retention policies, litigation hold and the recycle bin help within limited windows, and none of them give you what you actually want at the worst moment, which is the ability to say put this mailbox, or this SharePoint site, back exactly as it was on Tuesday morning. Deleted items age out. A user with permissions can destroy a lot of shared content quickly, and ransomware syncing through OneDrive will happily do the same.

The fix is unglamorous and cheap relative to the risk: an independent backup of Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, held separately from the platform itself, with retention you have actually chosen rather than inherited.

What we account for across Wales

Wales is a coverage question as much as a technical one. The distance between Cardiff, Swansea, mid Wales and the north is considerable, connectivity is uneven outside the urban areas, and there is a language requirement that does not apply elsewhere in our coverage.

Fixed-line options in rural and valley locations are frequently limited, and mobile coverage varies within a few miles. Designing for the connection that exists, with cellular failover and offline-tolerant working where needed, beats specifying for the connection you wish were there.

Organisations providing public-facing services may need to offer Welsh alongside English, which affects templates, forms, signatures and locale settings across the estate. Building it in from the start avoids a retrofit.

A large share of Welsh business touches the public sector somewhere, whether that is a health board, a local authority or a Welsh Government programme. Those relationships tend to pass their assurance expectations down the chain, so the questions arrive in a procurement pack rather than from your own risk register: how access is controlled, where data is held, what your recovery position is, and whether you hold a recognised certification. Being able to answer without a scramble is usually the difference between staying on a framework and quietly dropping off it.

Because our engineers travel from London and Stevenage, a visit to west or north Wales is scheduled rather than same-day. It also changes how we specify: more emphasis on remote diagnostics, on hardware that is unlikely to need physical attention, and on spare capacity held locally where a failure would stop the business.

Tourism, hospitality and agriculture give parts of Wales a pronounced seasonal shape, with headcount and transaction volumes that swing through the year. Licensing and capacity that suit August are wasteful in February, and the reverse causes outages. Reviewing that annually rather than renewing on autopilot usually saves more than any single technical change.

Where a connection is intermittent rather than slow, the design question changes from bandwidth to tolerance. Systems that assume constant connectivity will fail badly on a poor line, whereas ones that hold work locally and reconcile later will not. Choosing software that behaves sensibly offline, and keeping a mobile fallback that engages automatically, tends to matter more at a rural site than any upgrade to the primary line.

Businesses that scale up for a season need dozens of people productive quickly and gone cleanly afterwards. Done informally that means shared logins and accounts nobody closes. A prepared template for a seasonal role, created on arrival and expiring at the end of the contract, takes the same effort the first time and almost none thereafter, while leaving a clear record of who had access and when.

What we account for in Newcastle

Newcastle has a genuine digital and tech cluster alongside engineering and energy work connected to the Tyne. It is also the furthest of the areas we cover from our engineers, which we would rather address directly than gloss over.

Our engineers travel from London and Stevenage, so a same-day visit to Tyneside is a longer undertaking than one in the South East. In practice this makes remote resolution and good remote tooling more important, and it makes us more careful about specifying hardware that will not need hands on it.

CAD and simulation work needs specification and storage that ordinary office procurement underestimates, and the files are large enough to change how backup is designed.

Where a visit takes longer, spare capacity and a documented recovery path are worth more than they would be in a city with an engineer twenty minutes away. That is a design decision, not an upsell.

Work connected to the Tyne brings survey, inspection and design datasets that are large, retained for long periods and often gathered somewhere with poor connectivity before being brought back. That makes staged transfer and disciplined archiving more relevant than day-to-day office bandwidth.

Where a business runs telephone-based teams, availability of the voice path and its underlying connection is the service. Monitoring that reports on the network but not on call quality will miss the fault the business actually experiences.

Staff on a vessel, a rig or a remote site are not continuously connected, and treating that as a fault to be fixed usually fails. The better assumption is that work happens offline and synchronises when a link is available, with conflict handling that does not silently discard someone’s changes. It also affects security choices, since a control that depends on reaching a server in real time will lock out the person who most needs access.

Design and modelling work produces large files that several people revise. The failure mode is rarely running out of storage; it is two people working from different copies, or a reference file moving so an assembly no longer resolves. Check-out behaviour, a clear structure for references, and backups that capture a coherent point in time across the whole set are what prevent a day of rework.

Greater Manchester combines a professional-services core, a well-established media and broadcast cluster, and one of the larger digital and tech scenes in the UK. Each brings a different bottleneck, and they rarely overlap.

Production files are large, versioned and edited collaboratively, which strains both the connection and the backup window. Getting the storage tiering and sync rules right matters more here than raw device specification.

Guest access scoped to a single workspace or folder, with an expiry, covers almost every case and leaves nothing behind when the work finishes. Finished work that must be retrievable in three years is an archive question. Recovering yesterday’s state after something went wrong is a backup question. Payment redirection fraud targets exactly this mix of sectors, and it arrives by email rather than through the network. Authentication, impersonation protection and a firm rule about verifying bank details by telephone do more good here than additional perimeter spending.

Setting it deliberately is straightforward. Reconstructing it later, from mailboxes people have tidied and archives nobody documented, is the expensive version.

The safest change most professional firms can make is to stop moving sensitive documents as email attachments. A portal or a secure share means access can be withdrawn, viewing is recorded, and a message sent to the wrong recipient does not hand over the file. It also removes the temptation to protect a document with a password sent in a second email, which is not protection at all if both messages reach the same inbox.

What we account for in Bradford

Bradford has an unusually high proportion of owner-managed businesses and a manufacturing base rooted in textiles and food production. Many of them also operate across the Leeds corridor, which quietly turns a single-site business into a two-site one.

Owner-managed firms tend to ask what a line item prevents before approving it, which is a fair question. We would rather cost the things that stop the business working and be honest that the rest can wait than present a package where nothing is optional.

In smaller manufacturers the office switch and the machine on the floor are frequently the same network, because it grew that way. Separating them is usually the single highest-value piece of work available, and it rarely requires new hardware.

Staff moving between sites in the same week need their files, phone extension and permissions to follow them. That is an identity and cloud question rather than a networking one, and it is cheaper to solve properly than to work around.

Our engineers are based in Stevenage and travel north, so a Bradford visit is arranged rather than immediate. In practice most faults are resolved remotely long before a visit would arrive, and we would rather be straight about the travel than describe ourselves as local.

Much of Bradford’s commercial space is in converted mill and older industrial buildings, where thick stone walls, long cable runs and limited riser access constrain what a network can do. Wireless surveys in these buildings routinely produce different answers from the floorplan, and cabling work is often the unglamorous prerequisite to everything else.

A press or a production line bought fifteen years ago is often still perfectly serviceable, and still controlled by a PC running something no longer supported. Replacing the machine to solve a software problem is not a sensible answer. Isolating that PC on its own network segment, removing its need for internet access, and backing up its configuration is the pragmatic one. The goal is that an unsupported system cannot be reached from the office network and cannot reach anything else.

Office files are usually protected because they live in a cloud platform somebody manages. Production data frequently is not: machine configurations, job files, quality records and the small local database on the shop floor PC that nobody thinks of as a server. Those are the things that make a rebuild slow when hardware fails. Listing what a full recovery would actually require, then checking each item is covered, is a job worth doing once and reviewing yearly.

Birmingham pairs a dense professional-services core around Colmore Row with a manufacturing and engineering supply chain spread across the wider West Midlands. Those two halves of the city want very different things from IT, and a business often sits in both at once.

Serviced and multi-tenant buildings in the business district rarely let you touch the incoming connection or the risers. That pushes the design towards resilient wireless, cellular failover and cloud-first services rather than anything that assumes control of the building’s infrastructure.

Firms supplying automotive and aerospace primes increasingly find Cyber Essentials or an equivalent written into purchase terms. The certification itself is straightforward; the awkward part is usually the unsupported machine or shared login that has to be dealt with first.

Operations often run across Birmingham, Solihull and the Black Country, which makes consistency the real problem: the same policies, the same patch state and the same support route at every location, rather than three arrangements that grew separately.

Birmingham is one of the closer locations to our Stevenage base, so where hardware genuinely needs attention a same-working-day visit is a realistic commitment rather than a hopeful one. For manufacturers in the wider West Midlands, that is often the deciding factor.

Large-scale infrastructure and development work across the city has kept commercial relocation unusually frequent. Moves are where IT most often goes wrong, and the recurring cause is connectivity lead times booked too late rather than anything technical.

Operating across the conurbation often means each location grew its own arrangements, with separate logins, separate file stores and separate ways of doing things. Consolidating to a single identity per person, with access granted by role, removes most of the friction people feel when they move between sites and removes the accounts that accumulate when someone changes location. It also makes leavers a single action rather than a checklist per building.

Where work runs on a project basis, sites appear for a period and then stand down. Treating connectivity, hardware and access as something to set up and recover repeatedly, with a standard build rather than a bespoke one each time, keeps mobilisation quick and stops equipment quietly disappearing at the end of a job. The cost of a standard kit list is recovered the second time it is used.

Birmingham and the wider West Midlands hold one of the densest concentrations of manufacturing, logistics and professional services in the UK. Businesses of that kind rarely have a single tidy office: there is usually a mix of desks, a warehouse or workshop, and people who are rarely at either.

What unlimited actually means

Unlimited is a word worth pinning down before you sign anything, because plenty of providers use it and then quietly meter you. For us it means unlimited support requests. If your team needs help, they ask, however often that turns out to be. Nobody is counting tickets and nobody gets a bill at the end of the month for asking too many questions.

A project is still a project. Migrating you to a new system, fitting out a new office, rolling out fifty new laptops or building something from scratch is scoped and quoted separately, because the effort involved has nothing to do with day-to-day support and pretending otherwise would either cost you more every month or cost us the ability to do it well.

Hardware and licences are yours. We will advise, procure and manage them, often at better pricing than you would get direct, but the kit and the subscriptions are not hidden inside the support fee. We would rather tell you where the line sits now than have that conversation when something matters.

How we handle project work
Proactive, in practice

What proactive actually looks like

It is an easy word to say. Here is what it means in a normal month.

Monitoring that acts

Agents on your machines and servers report disk space, failing drives, missed backups, dropped services and security alerts. Thresholds create a ticket automatically, so the common ones get dealt with before anybody notices, rather than sitting on a dashboard nobody has open.

Patching on a schedule

Operating systems and third-party applications are updated on a defined cadence rather than whenever a user finally clicks the reminder. Unpatched software is still the most common way in, and patch management is one of the five Cyber Essentials controls for exactly that reason.

Assets and licences reviewed

We keep a live picture of what you own, how old it is and what it costs. That is how you avoid the two classic wastes: paying for subscriptions nobody uses, and running critical work on a machine that should have been replaced two years ago.

Response

What happens when you raise something

Every request lands in the same place and gets graded P1 to P5. A P1 is reserved for something that stops the business, like a total outage or a dead server, and gets immediate attention. Lower priorities still carry a committed response time, so nothing quietly rots at the bottom of a queue.

We’ll respond the same working day, and most issues are resolved on that first contact. When something genuinely needs hands on the hardware, one of our field engineers travels to you and we aim to be with you the same working day.

We deliberately keep our client list small rather than running thousands of accounts, which means the person picking up your ticket has probably worked on your systems before and does not need the whole history explaining again.

Overview

Mac support that actually understands Macs

Plenty of IT providers treat Macs as an afterthought. For Mac-first and creative teams, that means slow, frustrating support.

WhizzIT supports macOS properly, device management, security and support, whether you’re all-Mac or a mixed Windows and Mac environment.

Mac support runs on the same helpdesk, monitoring and patching stack as the rest of our support, so an all-Mac office and a mixed Windows and Mac estate are handled in one place rather than split between providers. Across 2025 our average first response time was 9 minutes and our average resolution time was 6 hours, measured across every ticket we handled. We are a team of five engineers supporting more than 30 UK businesses, from two-user teams to organisations of 150+ users. WhizzIT is Cyber Essentials certified and a Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider, so our security fundamentals are independently assessed rather than simply claimed.

Back to IT Support

What’s included

  • macOS support and troubleshooting
  • Mobile device management (MDM)
  • Endpoint protection for macOS
  • Microsoft 365 and Google on Mac
  • Onboarding and device setup
  • Mixed Windows and Mac environments
Device management

How a managed Mac fleet actually works

Most Mac problems in a business are not really Mac problems. They are the result of nobody managing the devices centrally.

Zero-touch setup

With Apple Business Manager and automated device enrolment, a Mac bought for a new starter can be shipped straight to them. It enrols itself the first time it is switched on, applies your settings, installs the apps they need and lands ready to work. Nobody has to sit and build it, and nobody has to post it to us first.

Settings that stick

Configuration profiles let us set the things that matter once and have them hold across every device: full-disk encryption on, the firewall enabled, a sensible screen lock, and administrator rights given deliberately rather than by default. New Macs inherit the same standard automatically.

Updates and offboarding

macOS releases, browsers and business apps are kept current on a schedule instead of whenever someone gets round to clicking the prompt. When a device is lost, or someone leaves, it can be locked or wiped remotely and the licences reclaimed rather than quietly disappearing.

Mac and Windows together

Mixed environments break on identity, not hardware

Hardly any business runs on one platform only. Designers and developers want Macs, finance and operations are on Windows, and the two have to share the same files, the same email and the same security rules. When that goes wrong, it is almost never because the hardware cannot cope. It is because identity and file access were never joined up.

The fix is to stop treating Macs as visitors on the network. Connect them to the same directory everyone else uses, so a Mac user signs in with the same Microsoft 365 account, the same multi-factor authentication applies, and revoking access when someone leaves genuinely revokes it everywhere.

Keep shared files in SharePoint and OneDrive rather than a legacy file share, which is where cross-platform setups usually start to creak. Then test the practical things on both platforms instead of assuming they work. Printing, VPN and conditional access are the usual culprits.

We are a Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider, so the Microsoft 365 and Entra ID side is handled directly by us rather than through a reseller chain, and the Mac side is managed to the same standard as the PCs beside it.

Our managed cloud services
Security

Macs are not exempt

The idea that Macs do not get malware is comfortably out of date. macOS is actively targeted, most commonly by information stealers dressed up as legitimate installers or browser downloads, which go after saved passwords, browser sessions and crypto wallets. The delivery method is usually a person being persuaded to run something, which is exactly why endpoint protection and user awareness both matter.

macOS does ship with some solid defences of its own. Gatekeeper and notarisation check what is allowed to run, XProtect removes known malicious software, and System Integrity Protection stops much of the operating system being tampered with. Those are a solid floor, not a managed security programme. None of them tell you that a device has stopped receiving updates, that encryption was switched off, or that someone has been granted admin rights they should not have.

The five Cyber Essentials controls apply to Macs exactly as they apply to Windows: firewalls, secure configuration, user access control, malware protection and patch management. We hold Cyber Essentials certification ourselves and take clients through it, and Macs are assessed alongside everything else rather than quietly left out of scope.

Healthcare providers combine special-category personal data with services that cannot simply pause. A clinic whose systems are unavailable is not inconvenienced; it is cancelling appointments and turning patients away, which makes availability a clinical concern rather than an operational one.

For a provider running clinics, the meaningful question is not whether a backup exists but how quickly a working system returns. Defining an acceptable recovery time, then testing against it, is the part that turns a backup into continuity.

Construction and the built environment

The office is fixed, the sites are not

Construction IT has to work in two places at once: a settled head office and a rotating set of sites that exist for months, have no fixed infrastructure and are frequently outside reliable coverage. Very little standard office IT design survives contact with that.

A new site typically has no fixed line and patchy mobile signal, yet needs drawings, variations and photographs moving the same day. Temporary connectivity, cellular failover and offline-tolerant working matter more here than raw office bandwidth.

Design files are big and change often, and building from a superseded revision is a costly mistake. The technology question is controlled access to the current version from a site device, which is a synchronisation and permissions problem rather than a storage one.

Site hardware is dropped, rained on and occasionally stolen. Device encryption, remote wipe and a fast replacement path are worth more than specification, because the realistic failure mode is loss rather than obsolescence.

What an audit covers

Findings are only useful if they are ranked

An audit that lists two hundred observations with no order of priority creates work rather than clarity. The useful output separates what exposes you now from what is untidy but harmless, and says what each fix costs in time and money so the decision can actually be made.

Almost every audit turns up the same category of surprise: devices nobody can account for, accounts belonging to people who left, software still installed after the project that needed it finished, and a licence count that no longer matches headcount. None of this is negligence. It is what happens when a business grows faster than its record-keeping. Establishing an accurate baseline is most of the value, because every later decision depends on knowing what you actually have.

A vulnerability on an internal print server behind a firewall is not the same as an exposed remote access service with a shared password, even if a scanner scores them similarly. Context decides severity: what the system touches, who can reach it, and what happens if it stops. We rank findings by that rather than by raw score, so effort goes where it changes the outcome.

How a new starter gets their accounts, how a leaver loses them, who approves a change, and whether anyone checks the backup restored are all process questions that no scan detects. They are also where most real incidents begin. An audit that only looks at boxes and software misses the half of the picture that people actually operate.

Findings are written to be read by a director as well as an engineer, with the reasoning visible rather than a bare list of severities. That matters when the audit exists because a customer, an insurer or a board asked for assurance, because the person asking is rarely the person who will implement the fixes.

Overview

Technology decisions that move your business forward

Without a plan, IT spend becomes reactive and disconnected from where the business is going. Good strategy turns technology into an advantage.

WhizzIT works with you to understand your goals and build a practical, prioritised roadmap, covering systems, security, cloud and budget, so every decision has a purpose.

Strategy work produces a prioritised roadmap tied to budget and business goals, reviewed as things change rather than written once and filed. The problem

The symptom is that you only think about IT when it breaks

If technology only reaches the agenda when something has gone wrong, then every decision gets made under pressure and usually costs more than it needed to.

A server fails and suddenly there is an unbudgeted five figure decision to make in a fortnight. A renewal lands that nobody knew was coming, on terms nobody negotiated. Laptops get replaced one at a time as they die, which is the most expensive way to do it. Somebody asks whether you are secure enough for a new client’s questionnaire and the answer is a shrug.

It is the absence of a plan, and it is entirely fixable. The point of strategy work is not a document that impresses people. It is knowing what is coming, roughly what it costs and roughly when, so decisions get made deliberately with time to shop around.

What tends to be missing

  • A refresh plan for hardware before it fails
  • A renewal calendar with dates and costs
  • Somewhere to see risks written down
  • A budget line for IT rather than surprises
  • A view of what growth will require
  • Evidence ready for client security questionnaires
Deliverables

What you actually get

Concrete outputs rather than a slide deck nobody opens twice.

A roadmap with dates and costs

A prioritised plan covering the next twelve to twenty four months. What needs doing, roughly what it costs, what depends on what, and what can safely wait. Written so a non-technical director can read it and make a decision, because that is usually who has to approve it.

A lifecycle and renewal picture

Every significant asset and contract with its age, its renewal date and its likely replacement window. This is the single most useful artefact for finance, because it turns IT from an unpredictable expense into a forecast you can plan around.

A risk register you can act on

The things that could genuinely hurt, ranked by how likely and how damaging, each with an owner and a next step. Not a list of theoretical threats. The unsupported server, the one person who knows how something works, the backup nobody has ever restored from.

The rhythm

Strategy is a habit, not a document

A plan written once and filed is worth very little. Businesses change, budgets move, a client asks for something new, and a roadmap drifts out of date within a couple of quarters if nobody revisits it.

Quarterly or half-yearly suits most businesses we work with: what did we plan, what actually happened, what changed in the business, what moves up the list. It usually takes an hour and it stops the plan quietly becoming fiction.

A technology audit or IT health check gives the roadmap something factual to stand on rather than assumptions about what is installed and how old it is. If you have never had that done, it is the sensible starting point.

The problem

AI is already being used across your business

Staff are already using artificial intelligence to draft emails, analyse data and summarise meetings, frequently before any formal governance exists. Adoption tends to happen quietly: different departments pick different tools, business data gets pasted into public platforms, and managers have little visibility into what’s being used.

The real challenge isn’t AI itself. It’s inconsistent adoption, undefined accountability and a lack of practical guidance. We help you introduce sensible oversight that balances innovation with information protection and management visibility.

Governance work sets out where AI tools may be used, what data may go near them and who signs that off, before shadow adoption sets the rules for you. Across 2025 our average first response time was 9 minutes and our average resolution time was 6 hours, measured across every ticket we handled. We are a team of five engineers supporting more than 30 UK businesses, from two-user teams to organisations of 150+ users.

The idea

What a SIEM is actually for

A SIEM does something quite specific: it gathers logs from everywhere, puts them into a common format, and looks for patterns across them that no single system could ever see on its own.

Your firewall records a connection from an unfamiliar country. Microsoft 365 records a successful sign-in for a finance account. An endpoint records a script running out of a temporary folder. Individually each one is unremarkable and would never justify waking anybody. In sequence, within nine minutes, they describe an attack in progress.

Correlation is the difference between having logs and being able to use them. Most businesses already produce all the evidence they need and simply have it scattered across six consoles that nobody compares, each retained for a different length of time, several of which quietly overwrite themselves.

What gets collected

  • Firewall and network device logs
  • Microsoft 365 and identity sign-in activity
  • Endpoint and server security events
  • Cloud infrastructure audit logs
  • Email security and filtering events
  • Administrative and permission changes
Honest answer

How this differs from MDR, and who is watching

These two get sold interchangeably and they are not the same thing. Managed detection and response is focused: it watches endpoints and identities for behaviour that looks like an attack and acts to contain it. SIEM and SOC is wide: it collects from everything, correlates across sources, keeps the history, and gives you the evidence trail. Most businesses start with MDR because it stops incidents. SIEM earns its place when you need to see across the whole estate, or you have compliance and audit obligations to satisfy.

In working hours alerts raise a ticket in our helpdesk and our engineers investigate. Outside those hours monitoring and first response are handled by a specialist partner we work with. We would rather set that out plainly than imply we run our own overnight operations centre, because a team our size cannot honestly staff three shifts and you can check.

Why retention matters

You cannot investigate what you never kept

When something does happen, the first question is always how long this has been going on.

Attackers wait

Intrusions are routinely weeks old before anything visible happens. If your firewall keeps a fortnight of logs and your endpoint tooling a month, the answer to how they got in may simply no longer exist. Centralised retention is what makes that question answerable.

Insurers ask

Cyber insurance applications increasingly ask directly whether you have centralised logging and monitoring. The answer affects your premium, and after an incident it affects whether a claim is straightforward. Being able to produce a timeline is worth a great deal at that point.

Auditors want evidence

Saying that only authorised people can reach the finance system is a claim. Showing who accessed it, when, from where, and what changed is evidence. Overview

Detecting and stopping threats in real time

Modern attacks move fast, often outside working hours. Prevention alone isn’t enough, you need to detect and respond quickly when something gets through.

WhizzIT’s MDR combines advanced tooling with expert analysis to detect threats across your endpoints and cloud and respond rapidly to contain them.

Detection and response covers your endpoints, Microsoft 365 identities, servers and cloud, with containment happening first so a problem stops spreading while it is investigated. Everything runs through the same UK service desk that handles your day-to-day tickets, so there is no separate team to chase. Across 2025 our average first response time was 9 minutes and our average resolution time was 6 hours, measured across every ticket we handled. The gap MDR fills

Antivirus asks one question

Have I seen this file before? That question works right up until an attacker uses something it has not seen, or does not use a file at all.

Someone gets hold of a working username and password, often from a convincing phishing page, and simply logs in. Nothing has to be installed, so nothing gets flagged. From there the attacker uses tools that are already on the machine, which is why this approach is known as living off the land. To antivirus it all looks like normal admin work.

MDR looks at behaviour instead of file signatures. It is less interested in what a file is called and more interested in what is happening: an account signing in from two countries an hour apart, a process quietly turning off protection, files being encrypted in bulk, a workstation suddenly scanning the rest of the network. Those patterns are hard to disguise, because they are the attack itself rather than the tooling used to deliver it.

How attackers move through a network

Behaviour we watch for

  • Sign ins from impossible locations or new countries
  • Multi-factor prompts being bombarded or bypassed
  • Files being encrypted in bulk
  • Endpoint protection or logging being switched off
  • New mailbox forwarding rules on finance accounts
  • One machine scanning or reaching across the network
Side by side

Traditional antivirus vs managed detection and response
